- architect: Designs system architecture and module boundaries before coding (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- backtesting-verifier: Reviews backtests for lookahead bias, data leakage, survivorship bias, overfitting, and implementation realism. Use after any strategy or backtest code change before trusting the results or promoting to paper/live trading. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- cicd-safety-auditor: Reviews CI/CD pipelines for flight software and safety-critical systems. Checks build reproducibility, artifact traceability, qualified vs unqualified tool separation, and compliance with DO-178C toolchain requirements. Use before any CI/CD configuration change or toolchain update. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- cpp-cmake-specialist: Handles C++17 implementation and CMake build system for the Silmulator's simulation core. Knows the project's C++ conventions, CMake structure, Python binding patterns, and performance-sensitive areas. Use for any C++ core or build system change. (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob)

- cross-platform-checker: Catches platform-specific assumptions that work on one OS but break on another — path separators, line endings, filesystem case sensitivity, platform APIs, shell assumptions. Use before any code that will run on both Mac and Linux (or Windows/Mac/Linux). (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- dependency-auditor: Checks that declared dependencies match actual usage across requirements.txt, CMakeLists.txt, package.json, and imports. Flags undeclared dependencies, unused declared dependencies, version drift, and security vulnerabilities in the dependency graph. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- deploy-checker: Verifies that a build actually produced the expected deliverables before declaring success — DMG built, installer works, web files render, binaries execute. Catches the class of failures where the build "succeeded" but didn't produce the thing you needed. (Tools: Read, Bash, Glob)

- devops-pipeline-reviewer: Reviews automation scripts, deployment pipelines, and infrastructure-as-code for reliability, idempotency, rollback safety, and audit trail quality. Specific to flight software DevOps concerns — not generic CI/CD advice. Use before any pipeline or infra change. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- execution-auditor: Reviews order management system (OMS) code for correct handling of fills, partial fills, cancels, and edge cases around market open/close. Use before any OMS change or when connecting to a new execution venue. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

"API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- explorer: Maps unfamiliar codebases and reports findings concisely (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- game-state-auditor: Reviews NPC action handling code to ensure proposed actions cannot corrupt game state. Focuses on the trust boundary between LLM output and C++ execution, validation logic, and edge cases in the action system. Use before merging any change to NPC action handling or the dialogue schema. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- hardware-spec-researcher: Given a real device model name, finds its SCPI command set from its programming manual and formats it for implementation in Silmulator. Use before implementing a new real-device simulator to ensure the command set is accurate. (Tools: Read, Write, Glob)

- market-data-validator: Validates market data ingestion pipelines for correctness, timezone handling, corporate action adjustments, missing bar detection, and stale data protection. Use before any data pipeline change and before running backtests on new data. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- misra-reviewer: Reviews C or C++ code against MISRA C:2023 and MISRA C++:2023 guidelines. Flags Mandatory, Required, and Advisory violations, identifies deviation candidates, and prepares findings for formal deviation records. Use on any safety-critical C or C++ code before review or static analysis tool runs. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- npc-dialogue-designer: Designs and implements NPC dialogue systems for the LLM-NPC game. - prompt-optimizer: Reviews and tightens NPC system prompts for token efficiency without losing character fidelity or schema compliance. - pyqt6-block-builder: Builds new hardware block components for the Silmulator PyQt6 drag-and-drop GUI. Knows the block pattern, canvas integration, signal/slot connections, and visual conventions. - requirements-tracer: Checks bidirectional traceability between system requirements, HLR, LLR, code, and tests. - scpi-implementer: Implements SCPI command handlers for new virtual devices in the Silmulator project. Knows the BaseDevice pattern, mandatory IEEE 488.2 commands, short-form aliasing, ErrorQueue behavior, and register conventions. Use when adding a new device class or extending an existing one's command set. (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob)

- software-lifecycle-doc-reviewer: Reviews DO-178C software lifecycle plans (PSAC, SDP, SVP, SCMP, SQAP) for internal consistency, completeness, and coherence with each other before DER review. Plans are where compliance breaks first — this agent catches the "plan says X but we're doing Y" gaps before they become audit findings. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- tester: Writes and runs tests for new or modified code (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash)

content.text:
You are running an overnight autonomous development session on this
repository. Use the overnight-coordinator agent to manage the full session.
You have full permission to read, write, commit, push, and open draft PRs.
You do NOT have permission to merge to main or close PRs after opening them.

## SETUP (run once at session start)

```bash
# 1. Ensure we are on main and up to date
git checkout main
git pull

# 2. Rebuild the knowledge graph so you navigate current code, not stale code
# (only if graphify is installed — skip silently if not)
graphify update . --force 2>/dev/null || echo "graphify not installed — skipping"

# 3. Check for a prior checkpoint (resume if interrupted)
cat .claude/memory/checkpoint.md 2>/dev/null || echo "No checkpoint — starting fresh"

# 4. Read tonight's issues
gh issue list --label "ready-for-ai" --json number,title,body,labels \
  --order created --limit 20
```

If a checkpoint exists and shows IN PROGRESS or FAILED stages, resume
from there rather than starting over.

Write the session start to .claude/memory/checkpoint.md:
```
# Checkpoint
Session started: [timestamp]
Goal: Work through all ready-for-ai issues
Status: IN PROGRESS
Issues to process: [list from gh output]
Issues completed: []
Issues failed: []
Issues skipped: []
```

---

## FOR EACH ISSUE (in number order, lowest first)

### A. READ AND ASSESS

```bash
gh issue view [N] --comments
```

Ask: Is this issue clear enough to attempt autonomously?

**Blockers that cause a SKIP:**
- Requires a design decision not documented in the issue
- Depends on another issue that isn't complete yet
- Requires credentials, API keys, or external resources not available
- Scope is too vague to produce a verifiable result

If blocked, label and move on — do NOT guess at intent:
```bash
gh issue edit [N] --add-label "needs-human" --remove-label "ready-for-ai"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Skipped overnight: [specific reason]. Please clarify before re-queuing."
```

### B. ORIENT

Invoke the git-historian agent:
"Use the git-historian agent to understand the code area this issue will touch."

This surfaces hot files, recent decisions, and things NOT to redo.
Read .claude/memory/history-brief.md after it completes.

### C. MARK IN PROGRESS

```bash
gh issue edit [N] --add-label "ai-in-progress" --remove-label "ready-for-ai"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Starting overnight implementation. Planning now."
```

### D. BRANCH

```bash
git checkout main
git checkout -b feature/issue-[N]
```

### E. PLAN

Use /plan-feature [concept from issue title] and wait for a plan.
Save the plan to .claude/plans/issue-[N].md

Do not implement until you have a written plan.

### F. IMPLEMENT

Use the appropriate specialist agents for this repo (see repo-specific
section below). Follow the plan. Write complete code — no placeholders.

If you hit a problem after 2 attempts on the same sticking point, SKIP
the issue and mark it ai-blocked. Do not spiral.

### G. TEST

Run the project's test suite. The exact commands are in the repo-specific
section below. Tests MUST pass before committing.

If tests fail after 2 fix attempts: skip, mark blocked, move on.
```bash
gh issue edit [N] --remove-label "ai-in-progress" --add-label "ai-blocked"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Blocked: tests failing after 2 attempts. [describe failure]. Needs human attention."
git checkout main
git branch -D feature/issue-[N]
```

### H. COMMIT AND PUSH

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "fix(#[N]): [issue title, shortened]"
git push origin feature/issue-[N]
```

### I. OPEN DRAFT PR

Generate the PR description using the /mr-description command, then:

```bash
gh pr create \
  --title "fix(#[N]): [issue title]" \
  --body "[output from /mr-description]" \
  --base main \
  --head feature/issue-[N] \
  --draft
```

Label the issue complete and close it with a reference to the PR:
```bash
gh issue edit [N] \
  --remove-label "ai-in-progress" \
  --add-label "ai-completed"
gh issue close [N] \
  --comment "Implemented. Draft PR open for review — see above."
```

### J. GENERATE LEARNING MATERIALS

**Identify the primary concept:**
Ask yourself: "What is the single most important technical concept a
developer would need to understand to maintain or extend this change?"

Guidelines:
- Choose the concept, not the feature name
  ("triple-channel SCPI addressing" not "E3631A support")
- Should be teachable in one lesson
- Should have testable recall in a drill
- Should introduce vocabulary worth learning

Then generate all three artifacts. In overnight/automated context:
- Generate the HTML files fully
- Skip in-chat interactive knowledge checks (no user present)
- Make the HTML content thorough — it is the only output
- Update PROGRESS.md with what was covered

```
/teach [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-[concept].html

```
/drill-me [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/drills/NNNN-[concept].html

```
/terms [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/vocab/NNNN-[concept].html
and updates docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md

Commit the learning materials on the same feature branch:
```bash
git add docs/learning/
git commit -m "docs(learning): add lesson, drill and vocab for [concept] (from issue #[N])"
git push origin feature/issue-[N]
```

### K. UPDATE CHECKPOINT

Append to .claude/memory/checkpoint.md:
```
Issue #[N]: [COMPLETED | FAILED | SKIPPED]
  Branch: feature/issue-[N]
  PR: #[PR number if opened]
  Concept taught: [concept]
  Learning files: lessons/NNNN-x.html, drills/NNNN-x.html, vocab/NNNN-x.html
  Notes: [anything notable]
```

Return to main: `git checkout main`

---

## END OF ALL ISSUES

### 1. Rebuild the learning index

```
/index
```

Commit:
```bash
git add docs/learning/index.html
git commit -m "docs(learning): rebuild index after overnight run $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
git push origin main
```

### 2. Write the morning report

Write OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md to the repo root:

```markdown
# Overnight Build Report
Date: [date]
Session duration: [start] to [finish]
Issues attempted: [N]

## Summary
[2-3 sentences on what was accomplished overall]

## Completed ✅
| Issue | Title | Branch | PR | Concept Taught |
|-------|-------|--------|----|----------------|
| #N | [title] | feature/issue-N | #PR | [concept] |

## Failed ❌
| Issue | Title | Failure Reason |
|-------|-------|----------------|
| #N | [title] | [why — specific, actionable] |

## Skipped (needs human) ⏭
| Issue | Title | Reason |
|-------|-------|--------|
| #N | [title] | [what needs clarification] |

## Learning Materials Created
| Concept | Lesson | Drill | Vocab |
|---------|--------|-------|-------|
| [concept] | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

## Test Status
[overall pass/fail and any notable failures]

## Suggested First Move
[The single most useful thing to do when you open your laptop]

## Draft PRs Awaiting Review
[list with PR numbers and one-line description each]
```

Commit and push the report:
```bash
git add OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md .claude/memory/checkpoint.md
git commit -m "chore: overnight report $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
git push origin main
```

---

## LEARNING CONCEPT SELECTION — GENERAL GUIDANCE

These guidelines apply to all repos unless overridden in a repo-specific
overnight-session command.

Choose a concept that:
- Is non-obvious (skip things any developer already knows)
- Will appear again in this codebase (worth learning for maintainability)
- Can be explained in one lesson without splitting into prerequisite lessons
- Has clear vocabulary (terms worth adding to the glossary)
- Produces useful recall questions in a drill

Avoid:
- Concepts named after specific model numbers or vendor names
  ("E3631A" is not a concept; "triple-channel PSU SCPI addressing" is)
- Concepts so generic they produce a useless lesson
  ("adding a class" — skip this)
- Concepts already well-covered in the existing lesson library
  (check docs/learning/PROGRESS.md first)

---

## FAILURE HANDLING POLICY

This policy applies to the entire session.

**Never stop the run because one issue failed.**
**Never silently skip — always label and comment.**
**Never attempt a risky or irreversible action without a prior commit.**

If at any point the session hits a situation that is genuinely ambiguous,
dangerous, or requires a human decision not covered by the issue:
1. Stop work on that issue
2. Label it needs-human
3. Leave a detailed comment explaining exactly what decision is needed
4. Move to the next issue

The goal is to maximize completed work, not to force through stuck issues.

---

## NOTE ON AUTOMATED LEARNING GENERATION

In a live session, /teach, /drill-me, and /terms end with in-chat
knowledge checks. In overnight autonomous mode, skip the interactive
questions and put that energy into making the HTML content more thorough
instead. The HTML is the deliverable — the in-chat conversation is not.

content.content:
1	# Plan: CSGO-Style Overhaul
2	Date: 2026-06-29
3	Status: READY FOR IMPLEMENTATION
4	Estimated complexity: L
5	
6	## The Idea
7	Transform the current open-arena wave shooter into a CSGO-inspired experience.
8	The arena is replaced with a single corridor-and-room map (T-side / mid / bombsite
9	layout). Textures go from flat checker/stripe to noise-based procedural concrete,
10	brick, and metal. The player can toggle between first-person and third-person cameras
11	with a keypress. Enemies no longer aim perfectly — each shot has a random spread
12	cone so they can miss. An ammo system (magazine + reserve) is added, requiring the
13	player to reload.
14	
15	## Goal
16	A player can load the game, explore a CSGO-style map in first or third person,
17	manage ammo, and fight enemies that miss shots at realistic rates.
18	
19	## Out of Scope (this version)
20	- Loading image files from disk (all textures remain procedural/in-code)
21	- Multiple maps or map selection
22	- Bomb/defuse game mode
23	- Buy menu or economy
24	- Multiplayer
25	- Shadows or dynamic lighting beyond the existing GL_LIGHT0
26	- Weapon switching / multiple weapon types
27	- Enemy pathfinding around walls (enemies will still move toward player;
28	  wall avoidance is a future issue)
29	
30	## Affected Areas
31	- `src/main.cpp` — all changes live here (single-file project)
32	  - `TextureSet` / `buildTextures()` — new procedural textures
33	  - `Player` struct — add `ammoInMag`, `ammoReserve`, `isReloading`, `reloadTimer`
34	  - `InputState` struct — add `reload` bool, `toggleCamera` bool
35	  - `GameState` struct — add `CameraMode` enum field
36	  - `renderScene()` — branch on camera mode for eye/target calculation
37	  - `drawArena()` — replaced by `drawMap()` with corridor geometry
38	  - `spawnEnemyShot()` — add angular spread
39	  - `spawnEnemy()` — replace random-anywhere with zone-based spawn points
40	  - `updatePlayer()` — ammo deduction on fire, reload logic
41	  - `renderHud()` — add ammo counter display
42	  - `readInput()` — add R=reload, V=toggle camera
43	  - New: `buildMapWalls()` returning `std::vector<MapWall>` defining the level
44	  - New: `drawMapWalls()` iterating the wall list
45	  - New: procedural texture generators: `makeNoiseTexture()`, `makeBrickTexture()`
46	
47	## Map Layout — "Dust" (one map, CSGO-inspired)
48	All units match the existing coordinate scale (kArenaHalfSize = 80).
49	
50	```
51	+--T-Spawn--+---Mid---+--A-Site--+
52	|           |         |          |
53	|  T-start  | central |  A bomb  |
54	|           |  open   |          |
55	+-----------+----+----+----------+
56	                 |   B corridor
57	            +----+----+
58	            |  B-Site  |
59	            +----------+
60	```
61	
62	Concrete implementation: a list of axis-aligned box walls (MapWall structs) that
63	`drawMap()` iterates and renders. No BSP or portal required at this scale.
64	Spawn zones:
65	- Player always starts at T-spawn centre (e.g. -60, 0, -60)
66	- Enemies spawn in A-site or B-site zones, never within 30 units of player
67	
68	## Implementation Order
69	
70	1. **Enemy miss chance** — modify `spawnEnemyShot()` to deflect the aim direction
71	   by a random angle drawn from a per-type spread cone. No other code changes.
72	   Grunt: ±8°, Sprinter: ±14°, Tank: ±4°. Commit: `feat(ai): add per-type aim spread`
73	
74	2. **Ammo system** — add `ammoInMag`/`ammoReserve`/`isReloading`/`reloadTimer` to
75	   `Player`. Add `reload` to `InputState`. Block firing when mag is empty.
76	   Decrement on fire. Reload on R (1.8 s). Add ammo readout to HUD.

# Plan: CSGO-Style Overhaul
Date: 2026-06-29
Status: READY FOR IMPLEMENTATION
Estimated complexity: L

## The Idea
Transform the current open-arena wave shooter into a CSGO-inspired experience.
The arena is replaced with a single corridor-and-room map (T-side / mid / bombsite
layout). Textures go from flat checker/stripe to noise-based procedural concrete,
brick, and metal. The player can toggle between first-person and third-person cameras
with a keypress. Enemies no longer aim perfectly — each shot has a random spread
cone so they can miss. An ammo system (magazine + reserve) is added, requiring the
player to reload.

## Goal
A player can load the game, explore a CSGO-style map in first or third person,
manage ammo, and fight enemies that miss shots at realistic rates.

## Out of Scope (this version)
- Loading image files from disk (all textures remain procedural/in-code)
- Multiple maps or map selection
- Bomb/defuse game mode
- Buy menu or economy
- Multiplayer
- Shadows or dynamic lighting beyond the existing GL_LIGHT0
- Weapon switching / multiple weapon types
- Enemy pathfinding around walls (enemies will still move toward player;
  wall avoidance is a future issue)

## Affected Areas
- `src/main.cpp` — all changes live here (single-file project)
  - `TextureSet` / `buildTextures()` — new procedural textures
  - `Player` struct — add `ammoInMag`, `ammoReserve`, `isReloading`, `reloadTimer`
  - `InputState` struct — add `reload` bool, `toggleCamera` bool
  - `GameState` struct — add `CameraMode` enum field
  - `renderScene()` — branch on camera mode for eye/target calculation
  - `drawArena()` — replaced by `drawMap()` with corridor geometry
  - `spawnEnemyShot()` — add angular spread
  - `spawnEnemy()` — replace random-anywhere with zone-based spawn points
  - `updatePlayer()` — ammo deduction on fire, reload logic
  - `renderHud()` — add ammo counter display
  - `readInput()` — add R=reload, V=toggle camera
  - New: `buildMapWalls()` returning `std::vector<MapWall>` defining the level
  - New: `drawMapWalls()` iterating the wall list
  - New: procedural texture generators: `makeNoiseTexture()`, `makeBrickTexture()`

## Map Layout — "Dust" (one map, CSGO-inspired)
All units match the existing coordinate scale (kArenaHalfSize = 80).

```
+--T-Spawn--+---Mid---+--A-Site--+
|           |         |          |
|  T-start  | central |  A bomb  |
|           |  open   |          |
+-----------+----+----+----------+
                 |   B corridor
            +----+----+
            |  B-Site  |
            +----------+
```

Concrete implementation: a list of axis-aligned box walls (MapWall structs) that
`drawMap()` iterates and renders. No BSP or portal required at this scale.
Spawn zones:
- Player always starts at T-spawn centre (e.g. -60, 0, -60)
- Enemies spawn in A-site or B-site zones, never within 30 units of player

## Implementation Order

1. **Enemy miss chance** — modify `spawnEnemyShot()` to deflect the aim direction
   by a random angle drawn from a per-type spread cone. No other code changes.
   Grunt: ±8°, Sprinter: ±14°, Tank: ±4°. Commit: `feat(ai): add per-type aim spread`

2. **Ammo system** — add `ammoInMag`/`ammoReserve`/`isReloading`/`reloadTimer` to
   `Player`. Add `reload` to `InputState`. Block firing when mag is empty.
   Decrement on fire. Reload on R (1.8 s). Add ammo readout to HUD.
   Commit: `feat(player): ammo and reload system`

3. **Camera toggle** — add `enum class CameraMode { FirstPerson, ThirdPerson }` to
   `GameState`. Add `toggleCamera` to `InputState` (key V). In `renderScene()`,
   branch: first-person eye = `player.pos + (0, 5.2, 0)` looking along
   `forwardFromAngles`; third-person keeps existing offset.
   In first-person mode, skip `drawPlayer()`.
   Commit: `feat(camera): toggleable first/third person`

4. **Improved procedural textures** — add `makeNoiseTexture()` (hash-based value
   noise for concrete) and `makeBrickTexture()` (row-offset brick pattern).
   Replace `gTextures.wall`, `.ground`, `.crate` assignments in `buildTextures()`.
   Commit: `feat(gfx): noise-based procedural textures`

5. **Map geometry** — define `struct MapWall { Vec3 center; float hx,hy,hz; GLuint tex; }`.
   Write `buildMapWalls()` returning the full wall list for the Dust layout.
   Write `drawMap()` iterating the list. Replace `drawArena()` call.
   Fix player start position in `startWave()` to T-spawn.
   Commit: `feat(map): csgo-style corridor map`

6. **Enemy spawn zones** — define two spawn rectangles (A-site, B-site).
   Update `spawnEnemy()` to pick a random zone then a random point inside it,
   rejecting if within 30 units of player.
   Commit: `feat(ai): zone-based enemy spawning`

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Pressing V toggles between first-person and third-person mid-game
- [ ] In first-person: player body is not visible; aim follows mouse look correctly
- [ ] In third-person: existing camera behaviour preserved
- [ ] Player starts each wave with 30 rounds in mag, 90 in reserve
- [ ] Firing when mag is empty does nothing; HUD shows 0/reserve
- [ ] Pressing R starts a 1.8s reload; cannot fire during reload
- [ ] After reload: mag refilled from reserve (or partially if reserve < 30)
- [ ] Enemy shots visibly miss the player at range (spread is perceptible)
- [ ] Map renders a T-spawn, mid, A-site, and B-corridor area with solid walls
- [ ] Enemies never spawn inside a wall or within 30 units of the player
- [ ] Procedural textures show concrete-like noise (not flat checkerboard) on walls
- [ ] Game builds cleanly: `mkdir -p build && cd build && cmake .. && make -j4`

## Edge Cases and Error Handling

| Situation | Expected behaviour |
|-----------|-------------------|
| Shoot with 0 ammo in mag, 0 reserve | No shot fired, no crash |
| Press R with full mag | No reload started (noop) |
| Press R with 0 reserve | No reload started |
| Toggle camera while dead/won | Camera still toggles (UI consistency) |
| Enemy spawn rejection loops forever | Cap retries at 50; if exceeded, skip spawn that tick |
| Wall count exceeds expected range | No runtime check needed — static list, always valid |

## Open Questions
None — plan is complete.

## Suggested GitHub Issues

1. `feat: enemy aim spread (miss chance)` — modify spawnEnemyShot with per-type cone
2. `feat: ammo and reload system` — Player struct, input, HUD readout
3. `feat: toggleable first/third person camera` — CameraMode enum + renderScene branch
4. `feat: noise-based procedural textures` — concrete, brick, metal generators
5. `feat: csgo-style corridor map geometry` — MapWall list, drawMap, player spawn fix
6. `feat: zone-based enemy spawning` — A/B site zones, 30-unit exclusion radius

# Skill: Procedural Textures (CPU-side OpenGL)

## When to use
When adding a new surface type that needs a distinct look without
loading image files from disk. All textures in this project are
generated in CPU memory and uploaded via `createTexture()`.

## The Pattern

```cpp
GLuint makeXxxTexture() {
    constexpr int kSize = 64;                          // always 64×64
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> pixels(kSize*kSize*4, 255);
    for (int y = 0; y < kSize; ++y) {
        for (int x = 0; x < kSize; ++x) {
            const int i = (y * kSize + x) * 4;
            // compute R, G, B
            pixels[i+0] = R;
            pixels[i+1] = G;
            pixels[i+2] = B;
            pixels[i+3] = 255;                         // always opaque
        }
    }
    return createTexture(pixels, kSize);               // defined in main.cpp
}
```

## Noise helper — `hashNoise(x, y, seed)`
Defined in `src/textures_proc.hpp`. Maps (x, y, seed) → [0,255] via
Wang hash. Deterministic, no `<random>` needed.

```cpp
// Two-octave grain example:
const float n = (hashNoise(x/8, y/8, 0) * 0.65f +
                 hashNoise(x/3, y/3, 1) * 0.35f) / 255.0f;
const std::uint8_t r = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(baseR + n * 24.0f - 12.0f);
```

## Existing generators (src/textures_proc.hpp)
| Function | Surface | Base colour |
|---|---|---|
| `makeConcreteTexture()` | load-bearing walls | grey (105,102,98) |
| `makeBrickTexture()` | site walls | terracotta (162,94,68) |
| `makeMetalTexture()` | cover objects | steel (100,100,108) |
| `makeGroundTexture()` | floor | warm tan (196,176,128) |

## Registering a new texture
1. Add a field to `TextureSet` in `main.cpp`
2. Write `makeXxxTexture()` in `textures_proc.hpp`
3. Assign in `buildTextures()`: `gTextures.xxx = makeXxxTexture();`
4. Bind with `bindTexture(gTextures.xxx)` before drawing

## Tile scale guideline
- Large flat surfaces (floor, ceiling): `tileScale = 8.0f`
- Medium walls: `tileScale = 3.0f–4.0f`
- Small props / crates: `tileScale = 1.0f–2.0f`

## Gotchas
- `createTexture()` expects the pixel buffer to outlive the GL upload call —
  pass by const-ref and let it copy; do not pass a temporary.
- `GL_REPEAT` wrap mode is set automatically by `createTexture()`, so tiling
  just works as long as you pass `tileScale > 1`.
- Adding a new texture does not require touching `CMakeLists.txt`.

Angular Spread & Aim Deviation in FPS AI

Issue #1AI behaviourMath

This lesson explains how to give enemy projectiles a realistic spread cone so that enemies miss the player at range — without making the miss feel random or unfair. The technique used in spawnEnemyShot() generalises to any FPS or third-person shooter.

Why Perfect Aim Is Bad Design

A mathematically perfect enemy always aims at the player's exact position. This feels unfair at long range (no skill matters) and trivial at short range (everything hits anyway). Real FPS games solve this with a spread cone: a maximum angle by which a shot can deviate from perfect aim.

Enemy TypeSpread (°)Design reason
Grunt±8°Average soldier — misses sometimes at range
Sprinter±14°Rushes in close; bad at ranged aim
Tank±4°Slow and deliberate — very accurate

The Geometric Model: Spread Cone

Imagine a cone with its tip at the muzzle, aligned along the perfect-aim direction d̂. The half-angle of the cone is the spread value θ. A valid shot direction is any unit vector that lies inside this cone. 

                   /----------\
                  /  spread θ  \
       muzzle ---+---- d̂ ------+--->  perfect aim
                  \            /
                   \----------/

To sample a random direction inside the cone we need three things:

  1. The perfect-aim unit vector d̂
  2. A random rotation axis perpendicular to d̂
  3. A random rotation angle in [-θ, +θ]

The Implementation in cpp_shooter_game

The code in spawnEnemyShot() uses a compact but effective technique: it perturbs the aim direction by adding a small random vector, then renormalises. This produces a biased-toward-centre distribution (shots are more likely to cluster near the centre of the cone), which happens to feel more natural than uniform cone sampling for most FPS games. 

// Per-type spread cone: deflect aim by a random angle within [-spread, +spread].
const float spreadDeg = (enemy.type == EnemyType::Sprinter) ? 14.0f
                      : (enemy.type == EnemyType::Tank)     ?  4.0f : 8.0f;
const Vec3 dir = normalize(aimDir + Vec3{randomFloat(-1.0f, 1.0f),
                                           randomFloat(-1.0f, 1.0f),
                                           randomFloat(-1.0f, 1.0f)} * std::tan(degToRad(spreadDeg)));

Why tan(spreadDeg)?

Consider a 2D version: the aim vector is (0, 1) and we add a horizontal perturbation p. The actual deviation angle is atan(p). To make the maximum deviation equal θ we need p = tan(θ). Using tan(spreadDeg) as the scale on the random perturbation ensures that the maximum possible deviation angle matches the specified spread — assuming the perturbation vector has magnitude at most 1 (true for values drawn from [-1, +1] but only in the worst case corner of the cube).

Caveat: The 3D version using three independent random components oversamples diagonal directions slightly (the cube corners are further from centre than the face centres). For a game-feel spread cone this is imperceptible, but for ballistic simulation you'd want proper polar-coordinate sampling.

Alternative: Uniform Cone Sampling

For a uniform distribution over the cone surface, use polar coordinates in the perpendicular plane: 

// Build a basis perpendicular to aimDir
const Vec3 perpA = normalize(cross(aimDir,
    std::abs(aimDir.y) < 0.9f ? Vec3{0,1,0} : Vec3{1,0,0}));
const Vec3 perpB = normalize(cross(aimDir, perpA));

// Sample a random point on the disc of radius tan(θ)
const float theta = degToRad(randomFloat(0, spreadDeg));
const float phi   = randomFloat(0, 2.0f * kPi);
const Vec3  dir   = normalize(aimDir
    + (perpA * std::cos(phi) + perpB * std::sin(phi)) * std::tan(theta));

This is more mathematically correct but requires more code and a separate random uniform draw for phi. The simpler version in the codebase is preferred for gameplay.

Tuning Spread for Feel

Design rule of thumb: multiply the intended miss chance at max engagement range by 2 to get a good starting spread angle. A Grunt at 50 units range with ±8° spread will miss roughly 30–40% of shots, which feels fair without being trivial.
Spread °Feel at 40 unitsUse for
±2–4°Nearly perfect — rarely missesSniper, Tank
±6–10°Moderate — misses at rangeStandard infantry
±12–18°Wide — often misses, close-range threatRusher, shotgunner
±25°+Very inaccurate — scary in numbersZombie horde

Key Vocabulary

  • Spread cone — the solid angle region within which a shot may deviate from perfect aim.
  • Half-angle — the spread value θ measured from the centre direction to the cone edge.
  • Perturbation — adding a small random vector to a direction before renormalising.
  • Ternary chain — the idiomatic C++ way to express a per-type constant without a switch.

Grunt±8°Average soldier — misses sometimes at range
Sprinter±14°Rushes in close; bad at ranged aim
Tank±4°Slow and deliberate — very accurate

The Geometric Model: Spread Cone

Imagine a cone with its tip at the muzzle, aligned along the perfect-aim direction d̂. The half-angle of the cone is the spread value θ. A valid shot direction is any unit vector that lies inside this cone. 

                   /----------\
                  /  spread θ  \
       muzzle ---+---- d̂ ------+--->  perfect aim
                  \            /
                   \----------/

To sample a random direction inside the cone we need three things:

  1. The perfect-aim unit vector d̂
  2. A random rotation axis perpendicular to d̂
  3. A random rotation angle in [-θ, +θ]

The Implementation in cpp_shooter_game

The code in spawnEnemyShot() uses a compact but effective technique: it perturbs the aim direction by adding a small random vector, then renormalises. This produces a biased-toward-centre distribution (shots are more likely to cluster near the centre of the cone), which happens to feel more natural than uniform cone sampling for most FPS games. 

// Per-type spread cone: deflect aim by a random angle within [-spread, +spread].
const float spreadDeg = (enemy.type == EnemyType::Sprinter) ? 14.0f
                      : (enemy.type == EnemyType::Tank)     ?  4.0f : 8.0f;
const Vec3 dir = normalize(aimDir + Vec3{randomFloat(-1.0f, 1.0f),
                                           randomFloat(-1.0f, 1.0f),
                                           randomFloat(-1.0f, 1.0f)} * std::tan(degToRad(spreadDeg)));

Why tan(spreadDeg)?

Consider a 2D version: the aim vector is (0, 1) and we add a horizontal perturbation p. The actual deviation angle is atan(p). To make the maximum deviation equal θ we need p = tan(θ). Using tan(spreadDeg) as the scale on the random perturbation ensures that the maximum possible deviation angle matches the specified spread — assuming the perturbation vector has magnitude at most 1 (true for values drawn from [-1, +1] but only in the worst case corner of the cube).

Caveat: The 3D version using three independent random components oversamples diagonal directions slightly (the cube corners are further from centre than the face centres). For a game-feel spread cone this is imperceptible, but for ballistic simulation you'd want proper polar-coordinate sampling.

Alternative: Uniform Cone Sampling

For a uniform distribution over the cone surface, use polar coordinates in the perpendicular plane: 

// Build a basis perpendicular to aimDir
const Vec3 perpA = normalize(cross(aimDir,
    std::abs(aimDir.y) < 0.9f ? Vec3{0,1,0} : Vec3{1,0,0}));
const Vec3 perpB = normalize(cross(aimDir, perpA));

// Sample a random point on the disc of radius tan(θ)
const float theta = degToRad(randomFloat(0, spreadDeg));
const float phi   = randomFloat(0, 2.0f * kPi);
const Vec3  dir   = normalize(aimDir
    + (perpA * std::cos(phi) + perpB * std::sin(phi)) * std::tan(theta));

This is more mathematically correct but requires more code and a separate random uniform draw for phi. The simpler version in the codebase is preferred for gameplay.

Tuning Spread for Feel

Design rule of thumb: multiply the intended miss chance at max engagement range by 2 to get a good starting spread angle. A Grunt at 50 units range with ±8° spread will miss roughly 30–40% of shots, which feels fair without being trivial.
Spread °Feel at 40 unitsUse for
±2–4°Nearly perfect — rarely missesSniper, Tank
±6–10°Moderate — misses at rangeStandard infantry
±12–18°Wide — often misses, close-range threatRusher, shotgunner
±25°+Very inaccurate — scary in numbersZombie horde

Key Vocabulary

  • Spread cone — the solid angle region within which a shot may deviate from perfect aim.
  • Half-angle — the spread value θ measured from the centre direction to the cone edge.
  • Perturbation — adding a small random vector to a direction before renormalising.
  • Ternary chain — the idiomatic C++ way to express a per-type constant without a switch.

input.content:
Magazine & Reserve Ammo State Machines

Issue #2Game mechanicsState machines

This lesson covers the two-pool ammo model used in CSGO and most modern FPS games, how reload state is tracked with a countdown timer, and the edge cases that break naive implementations.

Two-Pool Ammo Model

FPS ammo is split into two numbers that serve different purposes:

PoolWhat it representsIn cpp_shooter_game
Magazine (mag)Bullets currently loaded and ready to fire. Decrements on each shot.ammoInMag, max 30
ReserveSpare ammunition not in the gun. Only moves to the mag during reload.ammoReserve, starts at 90

The two-pool model creates meaningful decisions: do you reload now (wasting partial mag) or keep shooting with fewer rounds?

The Reload State Machine

Reload is a timed state — the player is locked out of firing for a fixed duration. The state machine has two states:

READY → R pressed, mag < full, reserve > 0 → RELOADING → 1.8s elapsed → READY

Transitions:

  • READY → RELOADING: R pressed AND mag not full AND reserve > 0
  • RELOADING → READY: countdown reaches 0 → partial or full refill
  • RELOADING (no transition): fire button pressed → no effect

The state is tracked with two fields in Player: bool isReloading (which state) and float reloadTimer (countdown to READY).

Partial Reload

When reload completes, the refill amount is the minimum of "rounds needed to fill the mag" and "rounds available in reserve": 

const int needed = kMagSize - game.player.ammoInMag;
const int take   = std::min(needed, game.player.ammoReserve);
game.player.ammoInMag    += take;
game.player.ammoReserve  -= take;

This handles three cases in one expression:

ScenarioResult
Full reserve (90), empty magmag = 30, reserve = 60

Issue #2Game mechanicsState machines

This lesson covers the two-pool ammo model used in CSGO and most modern FPS games, how reload state is tracked with a countdown timer, and the edge cases that break naive implementations.

Two-Pool Ammo Model

FPS ammo is split into two numbers that serve different purposes:

PoolWhat it representsIn cpp_shooter_game
Magazine (mag)Bullets currently loaded and ready to fire. Decrements on each shot.ammoInMag, max 30
ReserveSpare ammunition not in the gun. Only moves to the mag during reload.ammoReserve, starts at 90

The two-pool model creates meaningful decisions: do you reload now (wasting partial mag) or keep shooting with fewer rounds?

The Reload State Machine

Reload is a timed state — the player is locked out of firing for a fixed duration. The state machine has two states:

READY → R pressed, mag < full, reserve > 0 → RELOADING → 1.8s elapsed → READY

Transitions:

  • READY → RELOADING: R pressed AND mag not full AND reserve > 0
  • RELOADING → READY: countdown reaches 0 → partial or full refill
  • RELOADING (no transition): fire button pressed → no effect

The state is tracked with two fields in Player: bool isReloading (which state) and float reloadTimer (countdown to READY).

Partial Reload

const int needed = kMagSize - game.player.ammoInMag;

Magazine & Reserve Ammo State Machines

Issue #2Game mechanicsState machines

This lesson covers the two-pool ammo model used in CSGO and most modern FPS games, how reload state is tracked with a countdown timer, and the edge cases that break naive implementations.

Two-Pool Ammo Model

FPS ammo is split into two numbers that serve different purposes:

PoolWhat it representsIn cpp_shooter_game
Magazine (mag)Bullets currently loaded and ready to fire. Decrements on each shot.ammoInMag, max 30
ReserveSpare ammunition not in the gun. Only moves to the mag during reload.ammoReserve, starts at 90

The two-pool model creates meaningful decisions: do you reload now (wasting partial mag) or keep shooting with fewer rounds?

The Reload State Machine

Reload is a timed state — the player is locked out of firing for a fixed duration. The state machine has two states:

READY → R pressed, mag < full, reserve > 0 → RELOADING → 1.8s elapsed → READY

Transitions:

  • READY → RELOADING: R pressed AND mag not full AND reserve > 0
  • RELOADING → READY: countdown reaches 0 → partial or full refill
  • RELOADING (no transition): fire button pressed → no effect

The state is tracked with two fields in Player: bool isReloading (which state) and float reloadTimer (countdown to READY).

Partial Reload

When reload completes, the refill amount is the minimum of "rounds needed to fill the mag" and "rounds available in reserve": 

const int needed = kMagSize - game.player.ammoInMag;
const int take   = std::min(needed, game.player.ammoReserve);
game.player.ammoInMag    += take;
game.player.ammoReserve  -= take;

This handles three cases in one expression:

ScenarioResult
Full reserve (90), empty magmag = 30, reserve = 60
Reserve = 5, empty magmag = 5, reserve = 0 (partial)
Reserve = 0Reload never starts (pre-check blocks it)

Implementation in cpp_shooter_game

// Player struct fields added:
int ammoInMag   = kMagSize;           // 30
int ammoReserve = kStartAmmoReserve;  // 90
bool  isReloading = false;
float reloadTimer = 0.0f;

// In updatePlayer():

// 1. Count down the reload timer
if (game.player.isReloading) {
    game.player.reloadTimer -= dt;
    if (game.player.reloadTimer <= 0.0f) {
        const int needed = kMagSize - game.player.ammoInMag;
        const int take   = std::min(needed, game.player.ammoReserve);
        game.player.ammoInMag    += take;
        game.player.ammoReserve  -= take;
        game.player.isReloading  = false;
        game.player.reloadTimer  = 0.0f;
    }
}

// 2. Start reload on R key
if (input.reload && !game.player.isReloading
    && game.player.ammoInMag < kMagSize && game.player.ammoReserve > 0) {
    game.player.isReloading = true;
    game.player.reloadTimer = kReloadTime;  // 1.8f
}

// 3. Shoot only if armed and not reloading
if (input.shoot && game.player.shootCooldown <= 0.0f
    && !game.player.isReloading && game.player.ammoInMag > 0) {
    spawnPlayerShot(game);
    game.player.ammoInMag--;
    game.player.shootCooldown = 0.16f;
}

Edge Cases and Their Handling

Edge caseGuardResult
Shoot with 0 mag, 0 reserveammoInMag > 0No shot, no crash
Reload with full magammoInMag < kMagSizeNoop
Reload with 0 reserveammoReserve > 0Noop
Shoot during reload!isReloadingBlocked
R pressed while already reloading!isReloadingNoop (can't restart)

HUD Display

The ammo counter sits in the bottom-right, mimicking CSGO's layout. It changes colour during reload so the player has a clear visual cue: 

ammoStream << game.player.ammoInMag << " / " << game.player.ammoReserve;
if (game.player.isReloading) { ammoStream << "  RELOADING"; }
// Yellow tint during reload:
ammoText.setFillColor(isReloading ? sf::Color(255, 200, 60) : sf::Color::White);

Key Vocabulary

  • Magazine (mag) — the loaded ammo pool that depletes per shot.
  • Reserve — the unloaded ammo pool that feeds the mag during reload.
  • Reload state — a timed boolean state that blocks firing.
  • Partial reload — reload that completes with fewer than mag-size rounds (reserve exhausted).
  • Reload timer — a countdown float decremented each frame by dt; reaching 0 triggers completion.
  • Dead trigger — player pressing fire with an empty magazine; should be silently ignored.

Vocabulary: Angular Spread & Aim Deviation

Key terms from Issue #1 — enemy aim spread implementation.

Spread cone
The solid-angle region within which a shot direction is valid. Defined by its half-angle θ (the spread value). A shot can deviate from perfect aim by at most θ in any direction.
In cpp_shooter_game: spreadDeg is the half-angle; 8° for Grunt, 14° for Sprinter, 4° for Tank.
Usage: "The Grunt's spread cone has a half-angle of 8°, meaning shots stay within an 8° deviation from perfect aim."
Contrast with: shotgun spread (many pellets each with its own cone) vs. single-projectile spread (one shot per trigger pull).
Half-angle
The angular radius of a spread cone — measured from the centre direction to the edge of the cone. Also written as θ or the spread value.
In cpp_shooter_game: spreadDeg is the half-angle in degrees, converted to radians for std::tan().
Usage: "A half-angle of 14° means the maximum angular error is 14°, not 28°."
Aim perturbation
The technique of adding a small random vector to a unit direction and renormalising to produce spread. The random vector is scaled by tan(θ) so the angular deviation matches the desired spread.
In cpp_shooter_game: aimDir + Vec3{rand, rand, rand} * tan(spread) before normalising.
Usage: "The perturbation approach avoids building a perpendicular basis — just add noise and renormalise."
Contrast with: uniform cone sampling, which builds a perpendicular basis and samples a polar angle for an unbiased distribution.
Ternary chain
A C++ expression using multiple nested ternary (? :) operators to express a per-case constant without a switch statement. Idiomatic for small per-type constants in game code.
In cpp_shooter_game: (type == Sprinter) ? 14.0f : (type == Tank) ? 4.0f : 8.0f
Usage: "Use a ternary chain for three-case constants that don't warrant a switch or a lookup table."
Contrast with: switch statement (clearer for 4+ cases), lookup table (clearer when cases share structure).
Uniform cone sampling
A method to draw directions uniformly from a spread cone by constructing a perpendicular coordinate frame (basis vectors) and sampling a polar angle within [0, θ] and an azimuth in [0, 2π]. Produces a uniform distribution over the cone surface.
Not used in cpp_shooter_game (too complex for the payoff), but the lesson explains the algorithm for reference.
Usage: "For shotgun pellet patterns that need to look visually uniform, prefer uniform cone sampling over perturbation."
Contrast with: perturbation approach (simpler but slightly biased toward centre).
degToRad
Converts degrees to radians: deg × π / 180. Needed because C++ trig functions (sin, cos, tan) operate in radians.
In cpp_shooter_game: defined in the anonymous namespace in main.cpp. Used for spread, yaw/pitch, and camera math.
Usage: "Always pass radians to std::tan — use degToRad() to convert the designer-friendly degree value first."

Key points: Sprinter first (widest), Tank second, Grunt as fallback. Scale by tan not by spread directly.

Q6 — Written Recall

What is the difference between the perturbation approach used here and uniform cone sampling? When would you prefer the latter?

Perturbation approach: adds random Vec3 scaled by tan(θ), biased toward centre (less likely to sample near cone edge). Simple, 1-2 lines.

Uniform cone sampling: builds a perpendicular basis, samples a random polar angle/azimuth. Uniform distribution over the cone surface. More code (5+ lines), needs cross products.

Prefer uniform sampling when: the spread distribution matters for game balance (e.g., shotgun pellet patterns, trajectory visualisation, or recoil analysis tools). For simple AI miss-chance, the perturbation approach is fine.

cpp_shooter_game · Issue #1 · Drill: Angular spread in FPS AI

Angular Spread & Aim Deviation in FPS AI

Issue #1AI behaviourMath

This lesson explains how to give enemy projectiles a realistic spread cone so that enemies miss the player at range — without making the miss feel random or unfair. The technique used in spawnEnemyShot() generalises to any FPS or third-person shooter.

Why Perfect Aim Is Bad Design

A mathematically perfect enemy always aims at the player's exact position. This feels unfair at long range (no skill matters) and trivial at short range (everything hits anyway). Real FPS games solve this with a spread cone: a maximum angle by which a shot can deviate from perfect aim.

Enemy TypeSpread (°)Design reason
Grunt±8°Average soldier — misses sometimes at range
Sprinter±14°Rushes in close; bad at ranged aim
Tank±4°Slow and deliberate — very accurate

The Geometric Model: Spread Cone

Imagine a cone with its tip at the muzzle, aligned along the perfect-aim direction d̂. The half-angle of the cone is the spread value θ. A valid shot direction is any unit vector that lies inside this cone. 

                   /----------\
                  /  spread θ  \
       muzzle ---+---- d̂ ------+--->  perfect aim
                  \            /
                   \----------/

To sample a random direction inside the cone we need three things:

  1. The perfect-aim unit vector d̂
  2. A random rotation axis perpendicular to d̂
  3. A random rotation angle in [-θ, +θ]

The Implementation in cpp_shooter_game

The code in spawnEnemyShot() uses a compact but effective technique: it perturbs the aim direction by adding a small random vector, then renormalises. This produces a biased-toward-centre distribution (shots are more likely to cluster near the centre of the cone), which happens to feel more natural than uniform cone sampling for most FPS games. 

// Per-type spread cone: deflect aim by a random angle within [-spread, +spread].
const float spreadDeg = (enemy.type == EnemyType::Sprinter) ? 14.0f
                      : (enemy.type == EnemyType::Tank)     ?  4.0f : 8.0f;
const Vec3 dir = normalize(aimDir + Vec3{randomFloat(-1.0f, 1.0f),
                                           randomFloat(-1.0f, 1.0f),
                                           randomFloat(-1.0f, 1.0f)} * std::tan(degToRad(spreadDeg)));

Why tan(spreadDeg)?

Consider a 2D version: the aim vector is (0, 1) and we add a horizontal perturbation p. The actual deviation angle is atan(p). To make the maximum deviation equal θ we need p = tan(θ). Using tan(spreadDeg) as the scale on the random perturbation ensures that the maximum possible deviation angle matches the specified spread — assuming the perturbation vector has magnitude at most 1 (true for values drawn from [-1, +1] but only in the worst case corner of the cube).

Caveat: The 3D version using three independent random components oversamples diagonal directions slightly (the cube corners are further from centre than the face centres). For a game-feel spread cone this is imperceptible, but for ballistic simulation you'd want proper polar-coordinate sampling.

Alternative: Uniform Cone Sampling

For a uniform distribution over the cone surface, use polar coordinates in the perpendicular plane: 

// Build a basis perpendicular to aimDir
const Vec3 perpA = normalize(cross(aimDir,
    std::abs(aimDir.y) < 0.9f ? Vec3{0,1,0} : Vec3{1,0,0}));
const Vec3 perpB = normalize(cross(aimDir, perpA));

// Sample a random point on the disc of radius tan(θ)
const float theta = degToRad(randomFloat(0, spreadDeg));
const float phi   = randomFloat(0, 2.0f * kPi);
const Vec3  dir   = normalize(aimDir
    + (perpA * std::cos(phi) + perpB * std::sin(phi)) * std::tan(theta));

This is more mathematically correct but requires more code and a separate random uniform draw for phi. The simpler version in the codebase is preferred for gameplay.

Tuning Spread for Feel

Design rule of thumb: multiply the intended miss chance at max engagement range by 2 to get a good starting spread angle. A Grunt at 50 units range with ±8° spread will miss roughly 30–40% of shots, which feels fair without being trivial.
Spread °Feel at 40 unitsUse for
±2–4°Nearly perfect — rarely missesSniper, Tank
±6–10°Moderate — misses at rangeStandard infantry
±12–18°Wide — often misses, close-range threatRusher, shotgunner
±25°+Very inaccurate — scary in numbersZombie horde

Key Vocabulary

  • Spread cone — the solid angle region within which a shot may deviate from perfect aim.
  • Half-angle — the spread value θ measured from the centre direction to the cone edge.
  • Perturbation — adding a small random vector to a direction before renormalising.
  • Ternary chain — the idiomatic C++ way to express a per-type constant without a switch.

Relevant Code Location

skills.content:
You are running an overnight autonomous development session on this
repository. Use the overnight-coordinator agent to manage the full session.
You have full permission to read, write, commit, push, and open draft PRs.
You do NOT have permission to merge to main or close PRs after opening them.

## SETUP (run once at session start)

```bash
# 1. Ensure we are on main and up to date
git checkout main
git pull

# 2. Rebuild the knowledge graph so you navigate current code, not stale code
# (only if graphify is installed — skip silently if not)
graphify update . --force 2>/dev/null || echo "graphify not installed — skipping"

# 3. Check for a prior checkpoint (resume if interrupted)
cat .claude/memory/checkpoint.md 2>/dev/null || echo "No checkpoint — starting fresh"

# 4. Read tonight's issues
gh issue list --label "ready-for-ai" --json number,title,body,labels \
  --order created --limit 20
```

If a checkpoint exists and shows IN PROGRESS or FAILED stages, resume
from there rather than starting over.

Write the session start to .claude/memory/checkpoint.md:
```
# Checkpoint
Session started: [timestamp]
Goal: Work through all ready-for-ai issues
Status: IN PROGRESS
Issues to process: [list from gh output]
Issues completed: []
Issues failed: []
Issues skipped: []
```

---

## FOR EACH ISSUE (in number order, lowest first)

### A. READ AND ASSESS

```bash
gh issue view [N] --comments
```

Ask: Is this issue clear enough to attempt autonomously?

**Blockers that cause a SKIP:**
- Requires a design decision not documented in the issue
- Depends on another issue that isn't complete yet
- Requires credentials, API keys, or external resources not available
- Scope is too vague to produce a verifiable result

If blocked, label and move on — do NOT guess at intent:
```bash
gh issue edit [N] --add-label "needs-human" --remove-label "ready-for-ai"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Skipped overnight: [specific reason]. Please clarify before re-queuing."
```

### B. ORIENT

Invoke the git-historian agent:
"Use the git-historian agent to understand the code area this issue will touch."

This surfaces hot files, recent decisions, and things NOT to redo.
Read .claude/memory/history-brief.md after it completes.

### C. MARK IN PROGRESS

```bash
gh issue edit [N] --add-label "ai-in-progress" --remove-label "ready-for-ai"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Starting overnight implementation. Planning now."
```

### D. BRANCH

```bash
git checkout main
git checkout -b feature/issue-[N]
```

### E. PLAN

Use /plan-feature [concept from issue title] and wait for a plan.
Save the plan to .claude/plans/issue-[N].md

Do not implement until you have a written plan.

### F. IMPLEMENT

Use the appropriate specialist agents for this repo (see repo-specific
section below). Follow the plan. Write complete code — no placeholders.

If you hit a problem after 2 attempts on the same sticking point, SKIP
the issue and mark it ai-blocked. Do not spiral.

### G. TEST

Run the project's test suite. The exact commands are in the repo-specific
section below. Tests MUST pass before committing.

If tests fail after 2 fix attempts: skip, mark blocked, move on.
```bash
gh issue edit [N] --remove-label "ai-in-progress" --add-label "ai-blocked"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Blocked: tests failing after 2 attempts. [describe failure]. Needs human attention."
git checkout main
git branch -D feature/issue-[N]
```

### H. COMMIT AND PUSH

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "fix(#[N]): [issue title, shortened]"
git push origin feature/issue-[N]
```

### I. OPEN DRAFT PR

Generate the PR description using the /mr-description command, then:

```bash
gh pr create \
  --title "fix(#[N]): [issue title]" \
  --body "[output from /mr-description]" \
  --base main \
  --head feature/issue-[N] \
  --draft
```

Label the issue complete and close it with a reference to the PR:
```bash
gh issue edit [N] \
  --remove-label "ai-in-progress" \
  --add-label "ai-completed"
gh issue close [N] \
  --comment "Implemented. Draft PR open for review — see above."
```

### J. GENERATE LEARNING MATERIALS

**Identify the primary concept:**
Ask yourself: "What is the single most important technical concept a
developer would need to understand to maintain or extend this change?"

Guidelines:
- Choose the concept, not the feature name
  ("triple-channel SCPI addressing" not "E3631A support")
- Should be teachable in one lesson
- Should have testable recall in a drill
- Should introduce vocabulary worth learning

Then generate all three artifacts. In overnight/automated context:
- Generate the HTML files fully
- Skip in-chat interactive knowledge checks (no user present)
- Make the HTML content thorough — it is the only output
- Update PROGRESS.md with what was covered

```
/teach [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-[concept].html

```
/drill-me [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/drills/NNNN-[concept].html

```
/terms [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/vocab/NNNN-[concept].html
and updates docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md

Commit the learning materials on the same feature branch:
```bash
git add docs/learning/
git commit -m "docs(learning): add lesson, drill and vocab for [concept] (from issue #[N])"
git push origin feature/issue-[N]
```

### K. UPDATE CHECKPOINT

Append to .claude/memory/checkpoint.md:
```
Issue #[N]: [COMPLETED | FAILED | SKIPPED]
  Branch: feature/issue-[N]
  PR: #[PR number if opened]
  Concept taught: [concept]
  Learning files: lessons/NNNN-x.html, drills/NNNN-x.html, vocab/NNNN-x.html

```

Return to main: `git checkout main`

---

## END OF ALL ISSUES

### 1. Rebuild the learning index

```
/index
```

Commit:
```bash
git add docs/learning/index.html
git commit -m "docs(learning): rebuild index after overnight run $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
git push origin main
```

### 2. Write the morning report

Write OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md to the repo root:

```markdown
# Overnight Build Report
Date: [date]
Session duration: [start] to [finish]
Issues attempted: [N]

## Summary
[2-3 sentences on what was accomplished overall]

## Completed ✅
| Issue | Title | Branch | PR | Concept Taught |
|-------|-------|--------|----|----------------|
| #N | [title] | feature/issue-N | #PR | [concept] |

## Failed ❌
| Issue | Title | Failure Reason |
|-------|-------|----------------|
| #N | [title] | [why — specific, actionable] |

## Skipped (needs human) ⏭
| Issue | Title | Reason |
|-------|-------|--------|
| #N | [title] | [what needs clarification] |

## Learning Materials Created
| Concept | Lesson | Drill | Vocab |
|---------|--------|-------|-------|
| [concept] | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

## Test Status
[overall pass/fail and any notable failures]

## Suggested First Move
[The single most useful thing to do when you open your laptop]

## Draft PRs Awaiting Review
[list with PR numbers and one-line description each]
```

Commit and push the report:
```bash
git add OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md .claude/memory/checkpoint.md
git commit -m "chore: overnight report $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
git push origin main
```

---

## LEARNING CONCEPT SELECTION — GENERAL GUIDANCE

These guidelines apply to all repos unless overridden in a repo-specific
overnight-session command.

Choose a concept that:
- Is non-obvious (skip things any developer already knows)
- Will appear again in this codebase (worth learning for maintainability)
- Can be explained in one lesson without splitting into prerequisite lessons
- Has clear vocabulary (terms worth adding to the glossary)
- Produces useful recall questions in a drill

Avoid:
- Concepts named after specific model numbers or vendor names
  ("E3631A" is not a concept; "triple-channel PSU SCPI addressing" is)
- Concepts so generic they produce a useless lesson

Vocabulary: Magazine & Reserve Ammo State Machines

Key terms from Issue #2 — two-pool ammo model and reload state machine.

Magazine (mag)
The pool of bullets currently loaded and ready to fire. Decrements by 1 on each shot. Bounded by kMagSize.
In cpp_shooter_game: ammoInMag, starts at 30, max 30.
Usage: "The magazine empties on each shot — when it hits zero, firing is blocked until reload completes."
Reserve
The unloaded ammunition pool not currently in the weapon. Bullets move from reserve into the magazine only during a completed reload.
In cpp_shooter_game: ammoReserve, starts at 90.
Usage: "Reserve is the budget — once it is depleted, the player cannot reload even if the mag is empty."
Reload state machine
A two-state finite automaton (READY / RELOADING) that tracks whether the weapon can currently fire. Transitions are triggered by player input and by a countdown timer reaching zero.
In cpp_shooter_game: bool isReloading for state, float reloadTimer for countdown.
Usage: "The reload state machine ensures fire requests while reloading are silently discarded without corrupting ammo counts."
Reload timer
A countdown float decremented each frame by dt. When it reaches zero the reload state machine transitions back to READY and the partial-reload transfer executes.
In cpp_shooter_game: reloadTimer, duration kReloadTime = 1.8f seconds.
Usage: "Decrement the timer before checking start-conditions so that if the player somehow starts and finishes in one frame, neither branch races the other."
Partial reload
A reload where reserve has fewer bullets than the magazine needs to fill. The transfer is min(needed, reserve) — no bullets are created from nothing.
In cpp_shooter_game: const int take = std::min(needed, game.player.ammoReserve);
Usage: "Partial reload is the correct default — never unconditionally set mag to kMagSize, because reserve may not cover the difference."
Dead trigger
The player pressing the fire button with zero bullets in the magazine. Should be silently ignored — no sound, no animation, no crash.
In cpp_shooter_game: guarded by game.player.ammoInMag > 0 before the shoot branch.
Usage: "A dead trigger guard prevents negative ammo counts and is the first line of defence against fire-with-empty-mag bugs."
Reload guard
The compound condition that must be true before a reload is allowed to start: not currently reloading, magazine not full, reserve not empty.
In cpp_shooter_game: !isReloading && ammoInMag < kMagSize && ammoReserve > 0
Usage: "The reload guard prevents wasting time: reloading a full mag or a gun with no reserve are both no-ops."

First-Person vs Third-Person Camera Toggle

Issue #3Camera mathOpenGL

This lesson explains how a single camera setup — lookAt + perspective projection — serves both first-person and third-person views simply by moving the eye position. The insight is that what you look at stays fixed; only where you look from changes.

The Camera Model

OpenGL's view transform is defined by three vectors:

VectorMeaningFPS valueTPS value
eyeCamera position in world spacePlayer pos + up*eyeHeightPlayer pos − forward*back + up*up-offset
centrePoint the camera looks ateye + forwardDirPlayer pos (same!)
upWorld up direction(0,1,0)(0,1,0)

First-Person Camera

In first-person mode the eye sits at the player's head height directly above the player's position. The look-at target is one unit in front of the eye along the heading direction: 

// FPS eye sits at player position + eye height
const Vec3 eye = Vec3{
    game.player.pos.x,
    game.player.pos.y + kFirstPersonEyeHeight,   // 5.2f
    game.player.pos.z
};
const Vec3 fwd = forwardFromAngles(game.player.headingDeg, game.player.pitchDeg);
const Vec3 centre = eye + fwd;

The player model is invisible in this mode (it would occlude the view).

Third-Person Camera

In third-person mode the eye pulls back behind the player and rises slightly. The look-at target is the player's position — the camera orbits the player: 

// TPS eye pulls back along the flat forward direction and up
const Vec3 flatFwd = flatForward(game.player.headingDeg);
const Vec3 eye = Vec3{
    game.player.pos.x - flatFwd.x * kThirdPersonBack,   // 15.0f
    game.player.pos.y + kThirdPersonUp,                  // 8.0f
    game.player.pos.z - flatFwd.z * kThirdPersonBack
};
const Vec3 centre = game.player.pos;  // always look at the player

Switching Between Modes

The toggle uses rising-edge detection so a held key doesn't flip every frame: 

// Rising-edge detection — fires only on the frame the key is first pressed
static bool prevV = false;
const bool pressedV = sf::Keyboard::isKeyPressed(sf::Keyboard::V);
if (pressedV && !prevV) {
    game.cameraMode = (game.cameraMode == CameraMode::FirstPerson)
                    ? CameraMode::ThirdPerson
                    : CameraMode::FirstPerson;
}
prevV = pressedV;
Why static bool? The static keyword here gives the variable lifetime that persists across frames while keeping it local to the function. It holds the key state from the previous frame so the current frame can detect the rising edge (false → true transition).

Constants in camera.hpp

// src/camera.hpp
enum class CameraMode { FirstPerson, ThirdPerson };
constexpr float kFirstPersonEyeHeight = 5.2f;  // head above ground
constexpr float kThirdPersonBack      = 15.0f; // pull-back distance
constexpr float kThirdPersonUp        = 8.0f;  // height above player

These values sit in a header included before the anonymous namespace so they are available at global scope — they hold no function forward declarations, which is why they are safe to include early.

Why One gluLookAt Handles Both

gluLookAt constructs the view matrix from eye, centre, and up. The projection matrix (field of view, near/far planes) is unchanged between modes. This means the camera switch is a pure state change — no shader swaps, no render-pass changes, no separate camera objects.

Design insight: because the centre stays at or near the player in both modes, aim controls feel the same. The player just gains or loses the ability to see their own model. This is why games like GTA V can switch modes without rebinding any controls.

Key Vocabulary

  • Eye position — where the camera is in world space.
  • Look-at target (centre) — what the camera is aimed at.
  • Rising-edge detection — firing a one-shot action only on the frame a key transitions from not-pressed to pressed.
  • Static local — a local variable with persistent lifetime across function calls; used for inter-frame state.
  • flatForward — the heading direction projected onto the horizontal plane (y=0), used so the TPS pullback doesn't dig into the floor at steep pitches.

Vocabulary: First-Person / Third-Person Camera Toggle

Key terms from Issue #3 — camera modes and view-matrix setup.

Eye position
The world-space point from which the scene is rendered. The first argument to gluLookAt. Changing only the eye while keeping the centre and up the same produces a camera pan (dolly).
In cpp_shooter_game: FPS eye = player pos + (0, kFirstPersonEyeHeight, 0); TPS eye = player pos − flatFwd*kThirdPersonBack + (0, kThirdPersonUp, 0).
Usage: "The TPS eye is 15 units behind the player on the flat heading plane so steep pitch angles don't bury the camera in the floor."
Look-at target (centre)
The world-space point the camera is aimed at. The second argument to gluLookAt. Together with eye and up it fully specifies the view direction.
In cpp_shooter_game: FPS centre = eye + forwardDir; TPS centre = player.pos.
Usage: "In TPS mode the centre is fixed at the player — the camera orbits around them as heading changes."
Rising-edge detection
A pattern that fires a one-shot action only on the frame a boolean signal transitions from false to true. Implemented with a persistent previous-frame copy of the signal.
In cpp_shooter_game: static bool prevV compared against pressedV each frame; toggle fires only when pressedV && !prevV.
Usage: "Rising-edge detection is the standard fix for 'held key fires every frame' — it's also used for the V-key (view toggle) and any other single-fire input."
Static local variable
A local variable declared with the static keyword. Initialised once, persists across calls to the enclosing function. Used for inter-frame state without resorting to globals.
In cpp_shooter_game: static bool prevV = false; inside readInput() or the game loop.
Usage: "Prefer static locals over globals for inter-frame toggle state — they localise side-effects to the function that owns the toggle."
flatForward
The camera/player heading direction projected onto the horizontal plane (y = 0), then renormalised. Used when a horizontal-only displacement is needed regardless of vertical pitch.
In cpp_shooter_game: flatForward(headingDeg) — returns Vec3{sin(deg), 0, cos(deg)}.
Usage: "Always use flatForward for TPS pullback — using forwardFromAngles would pull the camera into the ground when the player looks down steeply."
CameraMode enum
A scoped enum (enum class) in camera.hpp with two values: FirstPerson and ThirdPerson. Stored in GameState and read by the rendering code each frame to select eye position.
In cpp_shooter_game: CameraMode cameraMode = CameraMode::FirstPerson; in GameState.
Usage: "An enum class prevents accidental comparisons against int literals — always compare with CameraMode::FirstPerson, never with 0."

Procedural Texture Generation & Wang Hash Noise

Issue #4Procedural generationHash functions

This lesson covers how to build CPU-side textures at startup using integer hash functions for pixel noise and bilinear interpolation for smooth variation — no image files required. The technique is used in textures_proc.hpp to generate all surfaces in the arena.

Why Generate Textures Procedurally?

Loading PNG/BMP files requires assets, asset pipelines, and disk I/O. For a small game engine or prototype, generating textures in code has three advantages:

  • Self-contained — no external asset files to bundle or misplace.
  • Parameterisable — change a seed or constant to get a different look without Photoshop.
  • Infinite resolution — generate at any size at startup without upscaling artefacts.

The Wang Hash — Fast Integer Noise

A hash function maps an integer to a pseudo-random integer in a way that is fast and deterministic. The Wang hash is a classic integer hash used in procedural generation: 

/** Wang hash: maps integer key to pseudo-random uint32_t. */
inline uint32_t wangHash(uint32_t k) {
    k = (k ^ 61u) ^ (k >> 16u);
    k *= 9u;
    k ^= k >> 4u;
    k *= 0x27d4eb2du;
    k ^= k >> 15u;
    return k;
}

/** Returns a noise value in [0, 255] for pixel (x, y) with a given seed. */
inline int hashNoise(int x, int y, int seed) {
    const uint32_t h = wangHash(
        static_cast(x) * 1619u +
        static_cast(y) * 31337u +
        static_cast(seed) * 1013u
    );
    return static_cast(h & 0xFFu);  // low 8 bits → [0, 255]
}

The per-pixel seed combines x, y, and a texture-specific seed so different textures using the same coordinates produce different noise patterns.

Bilinear Interpolation for Smooth Noise

Raw hashNoise produces fully white-noise (uncorrelated pixels). Smooth noise blends samples taken at a coarser grid using bilinear interpolation: 

/** Sample hashNoise at a coarse grid (stride s) and bilinearly interpolate. */
inline float smoothSample(int x, int y, int s, int seed) {
    const int  gx = x / s,    gy = y / s;
    const float fx = (x % s) / float(s),  fy = (y % s) / float(s);
    const float v00 = hashNoise(gx,   gy,   seed);
    const float v10 = hashNoise(gx+1, gy,   seed);

/** Wang hash: maps integer key to pseudo-random uint32_t. */
inline uint32_t wangHash(uint32_t k) {
    k = (k ^ 61u) ^ (k >> 16u);
    k *= 9u;
    k ^= k >> 4u;
    k *= 0x27d4eb2du;
    k ^= k >> 15u;
    return k;
}

/** Returns a noise value in [0, 255] for pixel (x, y) with a given seed. */
inline int hashNoise(int x, int y, int seed) {
    const uint32_t h = wangHash(
        static_cast(x) * 1619u +
        static_cast(y) * 31337u +
        static_cast(seed) * 1013u
    );
    return static_cast(h & 0xFFu);  // low 8 bits → [0, 255]

Vocabulary: Procedural Texture Generation & Wang Hash

Key terms from Issue #4 — CPU-side texture generation.

Wang hash
A fast integer-to-integer hash function that produces pseudo-random output from an integer key using XOR, multiply, and shift operations. Suitable for pixel-level noise because it evaluates in nanoseconds with no per-texture state.
In cpp_shooter_game: wangHash(uint32_t k) in textures_proc.hpp; called by hashNoise(x, y, seed).
Usage: "Prefer Wang hash over std::rand() for procedural textures — it's deterministic, seedable per-pixel, and produces no visible correlation between adjacent pixels."
hashNoise
A noise function that maps (x, y, seed) to an integer in [0, 255] by combining the coordinates into a single Wang hash key. Produces white noise (independent pixels).
In cpp_shooter_game: used directly for brick grain and metal streaks; used as the sample source for smoothNoise.
Usage: "Use hashNoise when you want fully uncorrelated pixel variation — detail grain, speckle, or dithering patterns."
Smooth noise (bilinear)
Noise with spatial coherence produced by sampling a coarse hash grid and bilinearly interpolating between grid points. Larger features emerge while pixel-to-pixel transitions remain smooth.
In cpp_shooter_game: smoothNoise(x, y, seed) blends two octaves (stride 8 at 65% + stride 3 at 35%).
Usage: "Use smoothNoise for surface variation that should look like concrete weathering or ground staining — areas, not dots."
Bilinear interpolation
Blending four values at the corners of a 2D grid cell using fractional coordinates (fx, fy). Formula: v00*(1−fx)*(1−fy) + v10*fx*(1−fy) + v01*(1−fx)*fy + v11*fx*fy.
In cpp_shooter_game: applied in smoothSample() to blend hashNoise values at grid corners.
Usage: "Bilinear interpolation is the minimum required to remove the blocky stepping that appears when you simply round to the nearest grid point."
Procedural texture
A texture whose pixel values are computed algorithmically at runtime rather than loaded from an image file. Generated once at startup and uploaded to GPU memory as a standard OpenGL texture.
In cpp_shooter_game: all textures (wall, ground, metal, brick, crate, player, enemy, projectile) are procedural, stored in TextureSet gTextures.
Usage: "Procedural textures eliminate asset pipeline friction in early development — swap the algorithm to change the look without touching any files."
RGBA pixel buffer
A flat array of unsigned bytes with 4 channels per pixel: Red, Green, Blue, Alpha. The format required by glTexImage2D(GL_RGBA, ...). Pixel at (x, y) in a W-wide image starts at index (y*W + x)*4.
In cpp_shooter_game: std::vector<unsigned char> px(W * H * 4) is the buffer type for all texture generators.
Usage: "The index formula (y*W + x)*4 is easy to get wrong — double-check W vs H ordering and the 4× multiplier whenever reading or writing pixel buffers."
Anonymous namespace include order
In this codebase, headers that forward-declare functions defined inside the anonymous namespace must be included inside the namespace, after the forward-declared function is defined. Violation causes a linker error for unresolved reference.
In cpp_shooter_game: #include "textures_proc.hpp" is placed after createTexture() inside the anonymous namespace in main.cpp.
Usage: "Treat this as a project convention: any header that calls functions defined in the anonymous namespace must be included inside it, after those functions are defined."

AABB Map Geometry for FPS Level Design

Issue #5Level designGeometry

This lesson explains how a flat list of axis-aligned boxes (AABBs) is used to represent FPS level geometry, how the room layout for the CSGO-style map is structured, and why axis-aligned representation is the right starting point for a prototype game engine.

What is AABB Geometry?

An AABB (Axis-Aligned Bounding Box) is a box whose edges are parallel to the world coordinate axes — no rotation. It is defined by a centre point and three half-extents (half-width, half-height, half-depth): 

struct MapWall {
    Vec3         center;     // world-space centre
    float        hx;        // half-extent along X
    float        hy;        // half-extent along Y (height)
    float        hz;        // half-extent along Z
    unsigned int tex;       // OpenGL texture handle
    sf::Color    tint;      // per-wall colour tint
    float        tileScale; // UV tile scale
};

A drawTexturedBox(center, hx, hy, hz, tex, tint, tileScale) call renders each wall by computing the 8 corner vertices and drawing 6 quads (one per face).

Why AABB First?

PropertyAABBArbitrary mesh
Definition6 numbers (cx, cy, cz, hx, hy, hz)N vertices + M faces
RenderingComputed on the fly per frameRequires VBO/VAO setup
CollisionTrivial interval overlap testRay-mesh intersection
Level editingChange 6 floatsRequires 3D modelling tool
LimitationsNo diagonal walls or rampsArbitrary geometry

For a CSGO-style prototype, AABBs produce the grid-based room structure that matches the original game's competitive map layouts.

The Level Layout

Z ^ | +--B-Site--+ | | | | +--B-Corr.-+ | | +---Mid----+--A-Site-+ | | | | | +--T-Spawn-+----+----+ +--------------------------> X
ZoneX rangeZ rangePurpose
T-Spawn−78 to −22−78 to −22Terrorist starting area
Mid−22 to +22−78 to +14Centre corridor
A-Site+22 to +78−78 to −14Bomb site A
B-Corridor−14 to +14+14 to +42Passage to B
B-Site−28 to +28+42 to +78Bomb site B

The MapWall List

buildMapWalls(wallTex, concreteTex, metalTex) returns a flat std::vector<MapWall>. Each element is one textured box. Rendering iterates the list: 

void drawMap(const std::vector<MapWall>& walls) {
    for (const auto& w : walls) {
        drawTexturedBox(w.center, w.hx, w.hy, w.hz, w.tex, w.tint, w.tileScale);
    }
}

This flat list is the simplest possible representation — no BSP tree, no spatial acceleration, no scene graph. For a small arena (<50 walls) the GPU overdraw is negligible and the CPU cost is zero.

Lambda Helper Pattern

Constructing many MapWall entries with the same height and tile-scale would be repetitive. A local lambda reduces noise: 

const float kWH  = 8.0f;  // wall half-height
const float kTS  = 6.0f;  // tile scale for wall texture
const float kFTS = 1.5f;  // tile scale for floor/ceiling

auto wall = [&](float cx, float cz, float hx, float hz, unsigned int tex) -> MapWall {
    return { Vec3{cx, kWH, cz}, hx, kWH, hz, tex, sf::Color::White, kTS };
};
Lambda default-argument rule: local constexpr variables cannot appear as default arguments in lambda parameters — this is a C++ limitation. The fix is to capture them and use them directly in the lambda body (as shown above).

Extending the Map

To add a new room or obstacle, add a MapWall entry to buildMapWalls(): 

// Example: a pillar at (50, 0, -40), 2 units wide, 8 tall, 2 deep
walls.push_back({ Vec3{50.0f, 8.0f, -40.0f}, 2.0f, 8.0f, 2.0f,
                  concreteTex, sf::Color::White, 3.0f });

No spatial index update is needed — the flat list is rebuilt once and used until the game ends.

Key Vocabulary

  • AABB — Axis-Aligned Bounding Box: a box with edges parallel to world axes, defined by centre + half-extents.
  • Half-extent — the distance from the centre to a face along one axis (hx, hy, hz); the full width is 2×half-extent.
  • MapWall — the project's AABB descriptor struct, carrying geometry, texture, tint, and tile scale.
  • drawTexturedBox — renders one MapWall by computing 8 vertices and issuing 6 quads in immediate-mode OpenGL.
  • Flat wall list — a std::vector<MapWall> iterated each frame; no spatial acceleration needed for small counts.
  • Tile scale — a UV multiplier; higher values repeat the texture more often over the surface (useful for large walls to avoid stretching).

The MapWall List

buildMapWalls(wallTex, concreteTex, metalTex) returns a flat std::vector<MapWall>. Each element is one textured box. Rendering iterates the list:
